summary: Defines SDP grouping semantics for redundant duplicated streams, a technique to recover from packet loss in real-time media, including at SSRC level. It works with the SDP grouping framework.

eli5.summary: Sending two copies of a message by different routes, so one arrives.

questions: what is dup grouping in sdp
how to group redundant rtp streams
subtitle: How SDP labels two or more copies of the same media stream so receivers can use one to repair loss in the other.

tldr.problem: Packets get lost even in carefully managed networks, and UDP multicast has no way to detect or retransmit them. Sending a duplicate stream helps, but SDP had no way to say which streams are copies of each other.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a DUP grouping semantic for the SDP a=group attribute, and a matching DUP semantic for a=ssrc-group when the copies share one RTP session through SSRC multiplexing.
tldr.outcome: A receiver that reads a DUP group knows the listed streams carry the same content and can combine them. A node that does not understand DUP answers without the grouping or refuses, and the sender then offers without duplication.

today: RFC 7104 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2014. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Duplicate a Stream
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) is widely used for IPTV and other real-time multimedia. Many such applications have very large numbers of receivers and rely on intra-domain UDP/IP multicast. Packet loss is not avoidable even in a carefully managed network. The RFC lists causes such as congestion, a flapping link, a link or interface failure, a software bug, or a maintenance person cutting the wrong fiber.

UDP/IP flows cannot detect loss or retransmit, so recovery is left to the RTP layer and the applications. One technique is to duplicate the packets and send them in separate redundant streams. This recovers from loss without the unbounded delay that would apply to all receivers. This RFC does not describe how to duplicate RTP streams. It only defines the Session Description Protocol (SDP) semantics needed to describe them.
sections.eli5: If a sender mails the same letter twice, one copy usually gets through. The receiver just needs to be told that the two envelopes hold the same letter.

sections.title: The DUP Grouping Semantic
sections.content:
An a=group line in SDP shows an association between streams. The streams listed on one such line are called a Duplication Group. Using the SDP Grouping Framework from RFC 5888, this document defines DUP as the semantics for redundant streams.

The a=group:DUP semantics MUST be used to group redundant streams, except when the streams are in the same media description (the same m line). The order of the listed streams does not strictly indicate transmission order. It is RECOMMENDED that the stream listed first be sent first, with the other streams being the time-delayed duplicates.
sections.eli5: A group line is a list that says: these streams are copies. The first one on the list should go out first, and the others follow a little later.

sections.title: Duplication for SSRC-Multiplexed Streams
sections.content:
RFC 5576 defines the ssrc-group media-level attribute for grouping RTP streams that are SSRC multiplexed and carried in the same RTP session. Because those streams sit in one m line, the group attribute cannot be used for them.

The meaning of DUP here is the same as for group, except that SSRC identifiers name the grouped streams. The syntax is a=ssrc-group:DUP *(SP ssrc-id). The same advice on ordering applies: the first listed stream is RECOMMENDED to be sent first.
sections.eli5: Sometimes both copies travel in the same envelope bundle. Then the list names each copy by its own number tag instead of by envelope.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Behavior
sections.content:
When duplication grouping is offered with the offer/answer model of RFC 3264, the sender cannot tell whether the other node lacks line grouping altogether or understands grouping but not DUP. Both cases look the same to the sender.

A node that does not support the grouping or the DUP semantics, following RFC 5888, responds in one of two ways: an answer that omits the grouping attribute, or a refusal such as 488 Not Acceptable Here or 606 Not Acceptable in SIP. After the first, the sender must send a new offer without duplication grouping. After the second, a sender that still wants the session should retry with an offer that has no duplication grouping.
sections.eli5: If the other side does not understand the copies note, it either ignores it or says no. Then the sender tries again without the note.

sections.title: The Three SDP Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives three examples, all carrying MPEG-2 transport streams (MP2T/90000) at port 30000.

  • Separate source addresses: the streams share one destination address but come from two source addresses, so the receiver must join both source-specific multicast sessions separately. The copies are grouped with a=ssrc-group:DUP 1000 1010.
  • Separate destination addresses: the streams are in two m lines with different destination addresses, grouped by a=group:DUP S1a S1b using the mid labels.
  • Temporal redundancy: both streams share source and destination addresses, so packets follow the same path. To survive loss, the duplicate of each packet is sent 50 milliseconds later, signalled by a=duplication-delay:50, an attribute defined in a separate draft.

The RFC notes that real SSRC values are random 32-bit numbers and can be much larger than the ones shown. It also notes that an a=duplication-delay:0 line MAY be added for information when no delay is applied.
sections.eli5: The examples show three ways to send the copies: from two different senders, to two different addresses, or down the same road with the second copy a moment later.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4566 apply. The RFC adds a weak threat: the duplication grouping could be altered to claim relationships that do not exist, which could make the duplication mechanisms fail or lead receivers to mishandle the streams.

To avoid this, the SDP description needs integrity protection and source authentication. The RFC mentions S/MIME, HTTPS, or the authentication method in the Session Announcement Protocol. If confidentiality is desired, a secure, encrypted transport can carry the SDP.

For IANA, the RFC registers the token DUP (Duplication) in two registries: the "Semantics for the group SDP Attribute" subregistry and the "Semantics for the ssrc-group SDP Attribute" subregistry.
sections.eli5: If a bad actor changed the copies note, receivers could get confused. So the note should be protected so nobody can tamper with it.

data.title: SDP with delayed duplication
data.code:
v=0
o=ali 1122334455 1122334466 IN IP4 dup.example.com
s=Delayed Duplication
t=0 0
m=video 30000 RTP/AVP 100
c=IN IP4 233.252.0.1/127
a=source-filter:incl IN IP4 233.252.0.1 198.51.100.1
a=rtpmap:100 MP2T/90000
a=ssrc:1000 cname:ch1a@example.com
a=ssrc:1010 cname:ch1a@example.com
a=ssrc-group:DUP 1000 1010
a=duplication-delay:50
a=mid:Ch1
